historical_timeline.summary: Riding fall in Culpeper, Virginia: fractures of the first and second cervical vertebrae with spinal cord injury; unable to breathe on his own.
Directed In the Gloaming; advocacy for disability and spinal cord research.
Physicians' report of late recovery to ASIA grade C; Nothing Is Impossible published.
Diaphragm pacing system implanted in Cleveland.

claims.statement: Christopher Reeve was born on September 25, 1952, in New York City.
He was an actor who became a household name in the title role of the 1978 film Superman.

On a Saturday at the end of May 1995, at 42, he was thrown headfirst when his horse stopped abruptly at the third obstacle of a cross-country event at an equestrian competition in Culpeper, Virginia. He was wearing a helmet. He broke his first and second cervical vertebrae, injured his spinal cord, and could not breathe on his own, as the University of Virginia neurosurgeon treating him reported.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic modern record of chronic C2 tetraplegia with ventilator dependence.

source_links.locator: broke the top two cervical vertebrae

claims.statement: After months of therapy he was able to breathe for short periods without a respirator. He became an advocate for people with disabilities and for spinal cord research, lobbied Congress for better insurance protection against catastrophic injury, and directed the film In the Gloaming in 1997.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his work as a director and advocate in the modern social history.

claims.statement: The Christopher Reeve Paralysis Foundation, built on his advocacy and fundraising, became a leading source of money for spinal cord research, and he helped establish the Reeve-Irvine research center at the University of California, Irvine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context for his advocacy; the modern episode names no foundation staff.

claims.statement: He wrote about his life after the injury in an autobiography, Still Me, and in Nothing Is Impossible: Reflections on a New Life (Random House, 2002), which described his activity-based therapy and his return to work.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own published accounts; the record uses only what reviewers of the books and the news reports summarize.

claims.statement: His physicians at Washington University reported his case in 2002: his injury was classified as C-2, ASIA grade A, with no substantial recovery in the first five years. An activity-based recovery program begun in 1999 was followed over three years by improvement to ASIA grade C, with motor scores rising from 0 to 20 of 100, sensory scores from 5-7 to 58-77 of 112, and voluntary control of some muscles including the right half of the diaphragm. Reversal of osteoporosis, more muscle mass and less spasticity were associated with the recovery, medical complications fell, and infections and antibiotic use fell by more than 90 percent.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His physicians' published account, with his public participation. Anchors the modern problem of incomplete C2 tetraplegia (ASIA C), the activity-based therapy, and the bone health plan.

claims.statement: In September 2002 the Associated Press reported that the first sign of change had been a movement of his left index finger almost two years earlier. He still used a wheelchair and a ventilator all but one hour a day and needed around-the-clock nursing care. He could feel about two-thirds of normal touch, which let him know when to shift his weight, so that he could sit in his wheelchair up to 16 hours a day without getting pressure sores. His program included electrically stimulated cycling for an hour three times a week and weekly pool therapy. Before it, his muscles had withered, his bones had thinned, and he had had repeated infections and life-threatening complications.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern pressure injury prevention, nursing care, exercise program and bone health plan.

claims.statement: In early 2003 surgeons at University Hospitals of Cleveland led by Dr. Raymond Onders implanted a diaphragm pacing system through small abdominal incisions. His phrenic nerves had not been injured. After eight years on a respirator, breathing through a tracheostomy, he could breathe for more than two hours without the respirator, and his doctors hoped the stimulation would let him wean further.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic modern episode, which begins some weeks after the implant, with a conditioning program to lengthen time on the pacer.

claims.statement: On October 9, 2004, he went into cardiac arrest at his home in New York and fell into a coma; he died on October 10, 2004, at 52. His publicist said he had been treated for a pressure wound, a common complication of paralysis, which had become severely infected and led to a serious systemic infection.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, after the modern episode; not used in it. The modern record keeps pressure injury prevention central for anyone with this injury.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care, coordinated with spinal cord injury medicine, for a 50-year-old director and advocate living with chronic incomplete C2 tetraplegia, ventilator use through a tracheostomy and a newly implanted diaphragm pacing system, on the Paralyzed Veterans of America Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine guidelines: recognizing autonomic dysreflexia and keeping a written plan with him and his nurses, pressure injury prevention with daily skin checks and the Braden scale, neurogenic bladder care with kidney surveillance by cystatin C and ultrasound, a daily bowel program, respiratory care with secretion clearance and a pacer conditioning schedule, vaccinations, venous thromboembolism awareness, bone health with DXA and vitamin D, spasticity and pain, cardiometabolic risk, mood screening, care team and equipment needs including power and ventilator backup, and advance care planning, with disability presented as part of a full working life.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week review, seen the same day by spinal cord injury medicine, with a bone density scan and kidney and bladder ultrasound

hpi.narrative: Mr. Reeve returns two weeks after his first visit and is seen by Dr. Kovac of physical medicine and rehabilitation on the same day. He uses the diaphragm pacer for two hours twice a day, as the pacing team advised, and the ventilator the rest of the time; he tires toward the end of each session but his saturation stays at 96 to 97%. His secretions are thin and his nurses suction a few times a day and use the cough-assist device each morning. His skin has stayed intact. His bowel program has worked each morning, and his catheter drains well. He has had no pounding headaches, flushing or sweating above the injury. His neck and shoulders ache after long days in the chair. He has continued stimulated cycling three times a week. All of his regular nurses have now been trained in the autonomic dysreflexia plan, and he carries the wallet card. He had his bone density scan and kidney and bladder ultrasound this morning.

referral.question: Chronic incomplete C2 tetraplegia (ASIA grade C) in a 50-year-old director and advocate who uses a ventilator through a tracheostomy and had a diaphragm pacing system implanted some weeks ago. Please advise on pacer conditioning, review his autonomic dysreflexia plan, bladder and bowel management, bone health, spasticity and pain, and his seating and equipment
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: Spinal cord injury in a riding fall eight years ago with fractures of the first and second cervical vertebrae. His physicians have published late recovery from ASIA grade A to C with an activity-based program of stimulated cycling and pool therapy, which he continues three times a week. A diaphragm pacing system was implanted laparoscopically in Cleveland some weeks ago; he now breathes on the pacer for up to two hours at a time and uses the ventilator otherwise. Indwelling catheter for neurogenic bladder; daily morning bowel program. Around-the-clock nursing care at home. No known autonomic dysreflexia episodes recently; a written plan and nitroglycerin ointment were set up today, and his baseline blood pressure is about 104/64. Today: weight 82.0 kg, pulse 62, saturation 97%; skin intact, Braden 11; PHQ-9 3; pain score 3 for neck and shoulder aching. Results today: white cells 7.2, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL; sodium 138, potassium 4.2 mmol/L; creatinine 0.48 mg/dL (low muscle mass); cystatin C 0.92 mg/L, eGFR 90; albumin 3.8 g/dL; calcium 9.0 mg/dL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL; PTH 52 pg/mL; A1c 5.5%; total cholesterol 172, LDL 104, HDL 34, triglycerides 170 mg/dL. A DXA of the hip and knee regions and a kidney and bladder ultrasound are booked for the morning of your visit. He directs his own care and decides who receives this letter
questions: How should his diaphragm pacer time be stepped up, and what should stop a session?
Is the written autonomic dysreflexia plan, with nitroglycerin ointment as the medicine of choice, appropriate for him?
Is his bladder management with an indwelling catheter and yearly ultrasound appropriate, and how should kidney function be followed?
What do you advise for bone health, given his history of osteoporosis that reversed with his recovery program?
Does his spasticity or neck and shoulder pain need treatment beyond his exercise program?
What seating, pressure-relief and equipment review do you advise?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Reeve, a 50-year-old director and advocate with a C2 spinal cord injury eight years ago, is seen at the request of Dr. Galloway. His physicians have published late recovery from ASIA grade A to C; he has sensation over much of his body and some voluntary finger and wrist movement, and continues stimulated cycling three times a week and weekly pool therapy. Some weeks after diaphragm pacer implantation he paces for two hours twice a day, tiring toward the end of each session, with saturation of 96 to 97%. His nurses suction a few times a day and use a cough-assist device each morning. He has an indwelling catheter and a daily morning bowel program, both working well. He has had no recent pounding headaches, flushing or sweating above the injury. His neck and shoulders ache after long days in his chair. His skin is intact. He wants to spend more time on the pacer and to keep working and traveling
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Galloway's intake note and the written autonomic dysreflexia plan. DXA this morning: total hip T-score -1.6, with low distal femur and proximal tibia densities. Kidney and bladder ultrasound this morning: no hydronephrosis or stones; mild bladder wall thickening with the catheter in place. Braden 11
